title: Design Tip #152: Slowly Changing Dimension Types 0, 4, 5, 6 and 7, Kimball Group (Margy Ross)
text:
Most Kimball readers know the core slowly changing dimension approaches: type 1 (overwrite the attribute), type 2 (add a new row to preserve history), and type 3 (add a column to hold a prior value). The Kimball Group also documents the less common types.

## Type 0: Retain Original
The dimension attribute value never changes, so facts are always grouped by this original value. It applies to durable identifiers and to attributes labeled original, such as a customer's original credit score, plus most date dimension attributes.

## Type 4: Add Mini-Dimension
Volatile or frequently analyzed attributes are split off into a separate mini-dimension table. A surrogate key represents each unique combination of those attribute values. Both the base dimension key and the mini-dimension key are carried as foreign keys in the fact table, enabling flexible grouping without bloating the primary dimension with rapid type 2 changes.

## Type 5: Add Mini-Dimension and Type 1 Outrigger
Type 5 builds on type 4. A current profile mini-dimension key is embedded in the base dimension and overwritten as a type 1 attribute. The moniker reflects that 4 plus 1 equals 5. This lets you access the current attribute values directly through the base dimension without joining through the fact table, but the ETL must keep updating this reference as the mini-dimension evolves.

## Type 6: Add Type 1 Attributes to a Type 2 Dimension
Type 6 combines type 2 row versioning with type 1 overwriting. Current attributes are embedded in and updated across all of an entity's prior type 2 rows, so facts can be filtered or grouped by either the historical value in effect when the measurement occurred or the current value. The type 6 name was suggested by an HP engineer in 2000 because it is a type 2 row plus a type 3 column that is overwritten as a type 1, and both 2 plus 3 plus 1 and 2 times 3 times 1 equal 6.

## Type 7: Dual Type 1 and Type 2 Dimensions
Rather than physically overwriting values, type 7 uses dual foreign keys in the fact table: one links to the type 2 historical version, and another links to the current row via the entity's durable natural key. This delivers type 6 style dual analysis without overwriting data.

title: Declaring the Grain, Kimball Group (Ralph Kimball)
text:
The Kimball four-step dimensional design process is: select the business process, declare the grain, identify the dimensions, and identify the facts. The answers are determined by considering the needs of the business along with the realities of the underlying source data during collaborative modeling sessions.

## Declaring the Grain Is the Pivotal Step
Declaring the grain means stating exactly what a single fact table record represents. A fact table record captures a measurement, and the declaration should be expressed in business terms, not technical database language. Ralph Kimball warns that the most frequent design error by far is not declaring the grain of the fact table at the beginning of the design process. Without it, the whole design rests on quicksand, and unauthorized facts and confusing dimension discussions creep in.

## Grain Must Come Before Dimensions and Facts
The grain must be declared before choosing dimensions or facts because every candidate dimension or fact must be consistent with the grain. This consistency enforces a uniformity on all dimensional designs that is critical to BI application performance and ease of use. A common mistake is to list dimensions and assume that constitutes a grain declaration. The correct approach anchors the grain to clear business objects and rules first, after which the appropriate dimensions become self evident.

## Examples of Grain Declarations
Atomic level grain examples include an individual line item on a customer's retail sales ticket as measured by a scanner device, a single transaction against an insurance policy, one line item on a medical bill, and an individual boarding pass for an airplane flight. Aggregated grain examples include monthly insurance policy totals by business line and weekly inventory measurements per product per store. For a doctor bill line item, Kimball identifies roughly ten potential dimensions: date, provider, patient, procedure, diagnosis, location, billing organization, responsible party, primary payer, and secondary payer, showing how atomic grain reveals extensive dimensionality.

title: Transaction Fact Tables, Kimball Group (Dimensional Modeling Techniques)
text:
A row in a transaction fact table corresponds to a measurement event at a point in space and time. Atomic transaction grain fact tables offer the maximum dimensional expressiveness, allowing extensive slicing and dicing.

Key characteristics of transaction fact tables: they may be dense or sparse because rows exist only when a measurement or event actually occurs; they consistently include a foreign key for each associated dimension; they may optionally contain precise timestamps and degenerate dimension keys such as an invoice or ticket number; and every measured numeric fact must be true to the transaction grain.

The transaction fact table is one of three fundamental fact table grains. A periodic snapshot fact table has a row that summarizes many measurement events over a standard period, so the grain is the period rather than the individual transaction. An accumulating snapshot fact table has a row for each occurrence of a short lived process with well defined milestones, and that row is revisited and updated as the process advances. Transaction fact tables are the most common type and are the primary workhorse schema for most organizations.

title: Periodic Snapshot and Accumulating Snapshot Fact Tables, Kimball Group
text:
## Periodic Snapshot Fact Tables
A row in a periodic snapshot fact table summarizes many measurement events occurring over a standard period, such as a day, a week, or a month. The grain is the period, not the individual transaction. Periodic snapshot fact tables are uniformly dense in their foreign keys because even if no activity takes place during the period, a row is typically inserted containing a zero or null for each fact. These tables often contain many facts, because any measurement event consistent with the fact table grain is permissible.

## Accumulating Snapshot Fact Tables
An accumulating snapshot fact table summarizes the measurement events occurring at predictable steps between the beginning and the end of a process. Pipeline or workflow processes, such as order fulfillment or claim processing, that have a defined start point, standard intermediate steps, and a defined end point can be modeled with this type of table. There is a date foreign key in the fact table for each critical milestone in the process. An individual row is initially inserted when the order line or item is created, then revisited and updated as pipeline progress occurs. This updating behavior is unique among the three fundamental fact table types, which otherwise never update rows once inserted. Accumulating snapshots typically also carry foreign keys for other dimensions, may include degenerate dimensions, and often contain numeric lag measurements and milestone completion counters.

title: Star Schemas and OLAP Cubes, Kimball Group (Dimensional Modeling Techniques)
text:
Dimensional models implemented in relational database management systems are referred to as star schemas because of their resemblance to a star like structure: fact tables in the center linked to a set of associated dimension tables via primary key to foreign key relationships. Dimensional models organize data into measurements, which are the facts, and descriptive context that represents the who, what, where, when, why, and how of an event, which are the dimensions.

Dimensional models implemented in multidimensional database environments are referred to as OLAP cubes. An OLAP cube contains dimensional attributes and facts, but it is accessed through languages with more analytic capabilities than SQL, such as XMLA. An OLAP cube can be equivalent in content to, or more often derived from, a relational star schema. A cube is often the final deployment step of a dimensional DW/BI system, or it may exist as an aggregate structure based on a more atomic relational star schema. Both star schemas and cubes share the same underlying logical dimensional design of facts surrounded by descriptive dimensions.

title: Snowflaked Dimensions (an anti-pattern), Kimball Group
text:
## What Snowflaking Is
When a hierarchical relationship in a dimension table is normalized, low cardinality attributes appear as secondary tables connected to the base dimension table by an attribute key. When this normalization process is applied repeatedly across all the dimension's hierarchies, a multilevel structure called a snowflake results.

## Why Kimball Discourages It
The Kimball Group advises against snowflaking for two primary reasons. First, it is difficult for business users to understand and navigate snowflakes. Second, snowflaking can negatively impact query performance. Although snowflakes represent hierarchical data technically accurately, the complexity works against the twin dimensional modeling objectives of simplicity and speed.

## The Denormalization Tradeoff
The key insight is that a flattened denormalized dimension table contains exactly the same information as a snowflaked dimension. Practitioners can therefore achieve the same informational content through denormalization while avoiding the usability and performance drawbacks of snowflaked structures. Snowflaking may reduce the disk space needed for dimension tables, but the savings are usually insignificant compared with the entire data warehouse and seldom offset the disadvantages. Designers must resist the normalization urge carried over from operational database design and instead collapse many to one fixed depth hierarchies into separate attributes on a flattened dimension row.

title: The 10 Essential Rules of Dimensional Modeling, Kimball Group (Margy Ross)
text:
Margy Ross of the Kimball Group lists ten essential rules that dimensional modelers should follow.

Rule 1: Load detailed atomic data into dimensional structures. Dimensional models should be populated with bedrock atomic details to support the unpredictable filtering and grouping required by business user queries.

Rule 2: Structure dimensional models around business processes. Business processes are the activities performed by your organization; they represent measurement events like taking an order or billing a customer.

Rule 3: Ensure that every fact table has an associated date dimension table. Every fact table should have at least one foreign key to an associated date dimension table whose grain is a single day.

Rule 4: Ensure that all facts in a single fact table are at the same grain or level of detail. Every measurement within a fact table must be at the exact same level of detail.

Rule 5: Resolve many to many relationships in fact tables. Because a fact table stores the results of a business process event, there is inherently a many to many relationship among its foreign keys, and those foreign key fields should never be null.

Rule 6: Resolve many to one relationships in dimension tables. Hierarchical fixed depth many to one relationships between attributes are typically denormalized or collapsed into a flattened dimension table.

Rule 7: Store report labels and filter domain values in dimension tables. The codes and associated decodes and descriptors used for labeling and query filtering should be captured in dimension tables.

Rule 8: Make certain that dimension tables use a surrogate key. Meaningless sequentially assigned surrogate keys deliver operational benefits, including smaller keys that mean smaller fact tables and buffered isolation from operational key changes.

Rule 9: Create conformed dimensions to integrate data across the enterprise. Conformed dimensions are essential for enterprise data warehousing; they support consistency and enable drill across from one business process to another.

Rule 10: Continuously balance requirements and realities to deliver a DW/BI solution that is accepted by business users. Dimensional modelers must straddle business user requirements along with the underlying realities of the associated source data.

title: Data tests, dbt Labs official documentation
text:
Data tests are assertions you make about your models and other resources such as sources, seeds, and snapshots. They are SQL select statements that seek to grab failing records, meaning rows that disprove your assertion. When you run dbt test, if the test returns zero failing rows it passes.

## Two Types of Data Tests
Singular data tests are the simplest form: a SQL query that returns failing rows, saved as a .sql file in the tests directory. For example, if refunds have a negative amount, a test can select order rows where the summed total amount is less than zero, and any returned row fails the test. Omit trailing semicolons and do not reference singular tests in YAML.

Generic data tests are parameterized and reusable, defined in a test block with arguments and referenced across many models via YAML. A generic not_null test, for instance, selects rows from the model where the given column is null.

## Four Built-in Generic Tests
dbt ships with four generic tests. unique asserts that values in a column have no duplicates. not_null asserts that a column contains no null values. accepted_values asserts that a column's values belong to a specified list, for example status in placed, shipped, completed, returned. relationships asserts referential integrity, that values in one column correspond to values in another table, for example customer_id maps to id in the customers model.

## Severity and Storing Failures
Tests support severity levels using the severity, error_if, and warn_if configs to control whether a failure raises an error or only a warning, for example warn_if greater than 5 and error_if greater than 10. Use the store_failures config or the --store-failures flag to persist failing rows to an audit schema for debugging. A best practice is that every model should have a primary key test, combining unique and not_null on the primary key column, and source data assumptions should be tested with accepted_values and relationships.

title: Sources, dbt Labs official documentation
text:
Sources in dbt represent data loaded into your warehouse by extract and load tools. Declaring tables as sources lets you select from source tables in your models using the source function to define data lineage, test your assumptions about source data, and calculate the freshness of source data.

## Declaring and Selecting Sources
Sources are defined in YAML nested under a sources key, each with a name, an optional database and schema, and a list of tables. In a model you reference a source with the source function, for example from source('jaffle_shop', 'orders'), which compiles to the fully qualified table name such as raw.jaffle_shop.orders. The source function also creates a dependency between the model and the source table, establishing lineage in the DAG. Using source references rather than hardcoding table names means a single YAML change updates every dependent model.

## Source Freshness
Source freshness helps monitor pipeline health and define SLAs. You configure it with a loaded_at_field, which is a timestamp column indicating when data was loaded, plus warn_after and error_after thresholds expressed as a count and period, for example warn_after 12 hours and error_after 24 hours. Running dbt source freshness constructs a query that compares the maximum loaded_at value to the current timestamp and reports a fresh, warn, or error state. You can then build only the models downstream of freshly loaded sources using a selector like source_status:fresher+. Freshness can be set to null on a table to exclude it from checks, and an optional filter avoids costly full table scans.

title: Materializations, dbt Labs official documentation
text:
Materializations are strategies for persisting dbt models in a warehouse. There are five built in types: table, view, incremental, ephemeral, and materialized view. By default dbt models are materialized as view, and you change this with the materialized config in dbt_project.yml, a config block in the model, or a properties YAML file.

## View
The model is rebuilt as a view on each run via create view as. Pros: no additional data is stored, and the view always reflects the latest source records. Cons: views that do significant transformation or that stack on other views are slow to query. Advice: start with views and only change when performance problems occur.

## Table
The model is rebuilt as a table on each run via create table as. Pros: tables are fast to query. Cons: they can take a long time to rebuild for complex transformations, and new source records are not automatically added until the next run. Advice: use for models queried by BI tools, and for slow transformations reused by many downstream models.

## Incremental
Incremental models let dbt insert or update only records that have changed since the last run. Pros: significantly reduce build time by transforming only new records. Cons: require extra configuration and are advanced usage. Advice: best for event style data; adopt when dbt runs become too slow, do not start with incremental models.

## Ephemeral
Ephemeral models are not built into the database. Instead dbt interpolates their code into dependent models as a common table expression. Pros: reusable logic and a cleaner warehouse. Cons: you cannot select from them directly, and overuse makes queries harder to debug. Advice: use for very lightweight transformations early in the DAG.

## Materialized View
The materialized view materialization creates and maintains a materialized view, combining the query performance of a table with the data freshness of a view, usually refreshed automatically on a cadence. Cons: they are more complex objects with fewer configuration options and are not supported on every platform.

title: About MetricFlow and the dbt Semantic Layer, dbt Labs official documentation
text:
MetricFlow is a SQL query generation tool that streamlines metric creation across different dimensions for diverse business needs. As part of the dbt Semantic Layer, it lets organizations define metrics using YAML abstractions so the same metric logic is written once and reused everywhere.

## Why Centralized Metric Definitions Matter
Without a semantic layer, multiple analysts working on the same data each write their own SQL, which leads to confusion, inconsistencies, and conflicting numbers in reports. MetricFlow moves the definition into version controlled YAML committed to the git repository, so the data and business teams can see and approve it as the single source of truth. This eliminates code duplication, inconsistent calculations across teams, and the manual SQL maintenance burden.

## Core Concepts
MetricFlow is organized around a semantic graph, the network of relationships between semantic models. Semantic models are the starting points of your data and correspond to models in your dbt project; they carry metadata such as the table name and primary keys. Entities are the join keys of a semantic model, the edges that let the graph traverse between models, and an entity can also act as a dimension. Dimensions are the ways you group or slice your metrics, and a dimension is an attribute of the table's primary or unique entity. Measures represent the quantitative columns aggregated by metrics. Metrics are the final business definitions, of several supported types, that you query with MetricFlow commands. The guiding principles are flexibility with completeness, DRY (do not repeat yourself), simplicity with gradual complexity, and performance.

title: Window Functions, PostgreSQL Documentation (Tutorial)
text:
A window function performs a calculation across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. This is comparable to the type of calculation done by an aggregate function, but unlike a regular aggregate, a window function does not cause rows to become grouped into a single output row. The rows retain their separate identities. Behind the scenes the window function is able to access more than just the current row of the query result.

## The OVER Clause
A window function call always contains an OVER clause directly following the window function's name and arguments. This syntactically distinguishes it from a normal function or non window aggregate. The OVER clause determines exactly how the rows of the query are split up for processing by the window function. For example, avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY depname) computes the average salary within each department while keeping every employee row.

## PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
The PARTITION BY clause within OVER divides the rows into groups, or partitions, that share the same values of the PARTITION BY expressions, and the function is computed across the rows of the current row's partition. You can also add an ORDER BY inside OVER to control the order rows are processed, which is what ranking functions such as row_number and rank depend on, for example row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY depname ORDER BY salary DESC). For each row a window frame is the set of rows within its partition that the function acts on; with ORDER BY the default frame runs from the partition start through the current row plus peers, and without ORDER BY the frame is the whole partition.

## Restrictions
Window functions are permitted only in the SELECT list and the ORDER BY clause. They are forbidden in GROUP BY, HAVING, and WHERE, because they logically execute after those clauses have already processed. To avoid repeating an identical OVER specification across several functions, define it once in a named WINDOW clause and reference it by name.

title: declutter! (and question default settings), storytelling with data blog (Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic)
text:
Clutter is made up of visual elements that take up space but do not add information, and it makes it harder for an audience to access the data. Clutter often creeps in unintentionally when designers fail to question their tools' default settings. The core principle is cognitive load: by reducing clutter, the audience can use their precious brainpower to decide what actions might be warranted rather than trying to figure out how to read the graph.

## Eight Decluttering Moves
Remove chart borders, since they add no information and white space differentiates a graph from surrounding elements just as well. Delete gridlines unless the audience needs to read exact values. Be sparing with data labels, applying them only when the exact numbers matter. Thicken bars so they are wider than the white space between them, which makes comparison easier. Title axes clearly and descriptively, for example percent of total births rather than just percent, and avoid diagonally rotated labels. Reposition legends directly adjacent to the data they describe instead of forcing the eye to move back and forth. Use color sparingly and strategically to focus attention rather than scattering it across many elements. Add a takeaway title that states the conclusion in words, because you should never assume different viewers will draw the same conclusion on their own. The overall philosophy is to strip everything that does not increase understanding so the data itself stands out.

title: Simpson's Paradox (an analysis anti-pattern), Wikipedia
text:
Simpson's paradox occurs when a trend appears in several groups of data but disappears or reverses when the groups are combined. It is also called the Yule Simpson effect, the amalgamation paradox, or the reversal paradox. The phenomenon is dangerous because aggregated frequency data can receive causal interpretations that flip once a confounding variable is accounted for.

## UC Berkeley 1973 Admissions
The classic example is graduate admissions at UC Berkeley in 1973. In aggregate, men were admitted at 44 percent versus 35 percent for women, appearing to show bias against women. When the data were stratified by department, the pattern reversed and showed a small but statistically significant bias in favor of women. The paradox arose because women disproportionately applied to competitive departments with lower acceptance rates, while men applied more to less selective departments; department difficulty overwhelmed the gender effect when the data were pooled.

## Kidney Stone Treatment
A medical example compares two treatments across stone sizes. For small stones Treatment A succeeded 93 percent of the time (81 of 87) versus Treatment B at 87 percent (234 of 270). For large stones Treatment A succeeded 73 percent (192 of 263) versus Treatment B at 69 percent (55 of 80). Treatment A is better in both subgroups, yet combined it appears worse: A at 78 percent (273 of 350) versus B at 83 percent (289 of 350). The confounder is stone severity, since doctors gave the tougher large stone cases to Treatment A.

## Lesson for Analysts
The direction of a relationship between two variables can increase, decrease, or reverse depending on which third variables are controlled. Resolving the paradox requires identifying the confounding variable and choosing the correct level of aggregation, not blindly trusting either the pooled or the segmented view.

title: Correlation and Causation, Australian Bureau of Statistics
text:
Correlation is a statistical measure, expressed as a number, that describes the size and direction of a relationship between two or more variables. Causation means that one event is the result of the occurrence of the other event, that is, there is a genuine causal relationship between the two events.

## Types of Correlation
The correlation coefficient r ranges from plus 1.0 to minus 1.0. A positive correlation means both variables move in tandem: as one increases the other increases, and as one decreases the other decreases. A negative correlation means the variables move in opposite directions. A correlation coefficient of 0 indicates there is no relationship between the variables.

## Why Correlation Does Not Equal Causation
A correlation between variables does not automatically mean that the change in one variable is the cause of the change in the values of the other. The relationship can be driven by a third variable. For example, sales of ice creams and sales of sunscreen can rise and fall together across a year in a systematic manner, but that relationship is due to the effects of the season, warmer weather, rather than any direct link between sunscreen and ice cream. Attributing causation to a correlation alone is a common analysis error.

## Establishing True Causation
The use of a controlled study is the most effective way of establishing causality between variables. In a controlled experiment, comparable groups receive different treatments, other influences are held constant or randomized, and the outcomes are compared, which isolates the effect of the variable of interest from confounders.

title: Cohort Retention Analysis, Amplitude Blog
text:
Cohorts are groups of users that share specific characteristics and usage patterns over a period of time. Cohort analysis groups users this way so a team can see how different segments behave across their lifecycle, which aggregate metrics hide.

## Acquisition versus Behavioral Cohorts
Acquisition cohorts organize users by when they joined or signed up, for example daily, weekly, or monthly signup cohorts, and they reveal when users leave after signup. In one music app example, of 11,528 users who signed up on July 16, only 49.7 percent were still active by day five. Behavioral cohorts segment users by past actions or profile characteristics, such as users who favorited songs or joined communities, and they reveal which behaviors correlate with retention, though correlation does not imply causation.

## The Retention Curve and Why It Beats Averages
Retention is measured with a cohort retention curve that shows the percentage of users in a cohort still active at each period after signup, exposing the critical drop off points in the user journey. Aggregate metrics miss the story. In the Amplitude example, roughly 40 percent of all users churned daily, but only about 15 percent of users who favorited three or more songs dropped off. That difference is invisible in a company wide average and points the team toward the behaviors worth driving during onboarding.

title: Common pitfalls and recommended practices (data leakage), scikit-learn official documentation
text:
## Data Leakage
Data leakage occurs when information that would not be available at prediction time is used when building the model. This results in overly optimistic performance estimates, for example from cross validation, and thus poorer performance when the model is used on actually novel data, such as during production.

The general rule is to never call fit on the test data. Always split the data into train and test subsets first, particularly before any preprocessing steps. Never include test data when using the fit and fit_transform methods, because using all the data can result in overly optimistic scores. The transform method should be used on both train and test subsets, since the same preprocessing should be applied to all the data, achieved by fit_transform on the train subset and transform on the test subset. Using a Pipeline prevents most data leakage by ensuring the appropriate method runs on the correct subset. A concrete example: fitting SelectKBest feature selection on the entire dataset before splitting produced an accuracy of 0.76 on random targets, while correctly fitting the selector only on the training split produced 0.5, the honest score expected for random data.

## Inconsistent Preprocessing
If data transforms are used when training a model, they also must be used on subsequent datasets, whether test data or production data. Otherwise the feature space changes and the model cannot perform effectively. In the documentation example, scoring test data that was not scaled with the fitted StandardScaler gave a mean squared error of 62.80, while applying the same transform gave 0.90.

## Controlling Randomness
If an integer is passed to random_state, calling fit or split multiple times yields the same results, which is usually the safest option for CV splitters and gives reproducibility across program executions. Passing None or a RandomState instance yields different results each call. To obtain constant results across runs you must remove all uses of random_state=None, which is the default.

title: Data Distribution Shifts and Monitoring, Chip Huyen
text:
Chip Huyen frames data distribution shifts using the joint distribution P(X, Y), where X is the input and Y is the output, decomposed either as P(X) times P(Y given X) or P(Y) times P(X given Y).

## Three Types of Shift
Covariate shift is when P(X) changes but P(Y given X) remains the same: the input distribution shifts while the relationship between inputs and outputs stays constant. Example: a breast cancer detection model trained on patients over 40 but deployed on a younger population. Label shift is when P(Y) changes but P(X given Y) remains the same: the output distribution changes while inputs conditional on outputs stay stable. Concept drift, also called posterior shift, is when P(Y given X) changes but P(X) remains the same: the same inputs produce different outputs over time. Example: COVID-19 caused housing demand and prices to change even though the property features were unchanged.

## Why Models Degrade in Production
Train serving skew means training data rarely matches production data because of collection biases and real world complexity. The real world is not stationary: distributions shift suddenly (a competitor changes pricing), gradually (cultural trends), or seasonally (weather). Importantly, a large percentage of what looks like data shift is actually caused by internal errors such as pipeline bugs or inconsistent feature extraction between training and serving.

## Monitoring
ML systems often fail silently, because performance degradation lacks the operational errors that traditional software throws. Huyen recommends monitoring artifacts at increasing depth in the pipeline: raw inputs, features, predictions, and accuracy related metrics when ground truth is available. Detection methods include statistical two sample tests such as the Kolmogorov Smirnov test and Maximum Mean Discrepancy on feature distributions.

title: How Not To Run An A/B Test (the peeking problem), Evan Miller
text:
Most A/B testing dashboards assume a sample size that is fixed in advance. When experimenters instead adopt a peek and stop approach, repeatedly checking results and halting as soon as significance appears, they violate that assumption and invalidate the reported significance level.

## False Positive Inflation
Evan Miller gives a stark example: testing whether a new logo affects a 50 percent conversion rate, stopping at 5 percent significance or after 150 observations, yields false positives 26.1 percent of the time, more than five times what you probably thought. He states the principle plainly: repeated significance testing always increases the rate of false positives. If you peek at an ongoing experiment ten times, what you think is 1 percent significance is actually just 5 percent significance. His correction table shows that to keep a true 5 percent false positive rate you must report at roughly 2.9 percent significance after 1 peek, 1.4 percent after 5 peeks, and 1.0 percent after 10 peeks.

## The Fix
Decide on a sample size in advance and wait until the experiment is over before you start believing the significance claims, applying near religious discipline about respecting the predetermined sample size. For valid continuous monitoring, use a sequential design with pre established checkpoints and corrected significance levels, or Bayesian methods that allow stopping at any time while maintaining valid inference.

title: Statistical Power, MDE, and Designing Statistical Tests, Georgi Georgiev (Analytics-Toolkit)
text:
Statistical power is the probability to reject the null hypothesis over the possible values of the parameter of interest. More precisely, the power at a given effect size is the probability of observing a p-value statistically significant at threshold alpha if a true effect of magnitude mu is in fact present. Power is really a curve across all possible effect sizes, not a single number, and calculating it requires only the sample size, the confidence threshold, and the variance, not a prediction of the true effect.

## Type I and Type II Error
The significance threshold alpha defines the Type I error probability, the chance of declaring a winner when there is no real effect. A common choice is 95 percent confidence, meaning alpha of 0.05. Power is the inverse of the Type II error rate beta at a specified effect size, so 80 percent power corresponds to a 20 percent chance of missing a real effect of that size.

## Minimum Detectable Effect versus Minimum Effect of Interest
The article carefully distinguishes two concepts that are often conflated. The Minimum Effect of Interest is the smallest practically meaningful effect worth detecting, set through a risk and reward analysis of business costs and benefits. The Minimum Detectable Effect is the true effect size at which a given, already specified test achieves a chosen power level. Sample size depends on three interconnected inputs: the confidence threshold, the minimum effect of interest, and the desired statistical power. Georgiev criticizes blindly using conventions such as 80 or 90 percent power without business justification, and instead advocates optimizing all three parameters jointly through risk and reward, since demanding a smaller detectable effect or higher power both require a larger sample.

title: Overfitting and Generalization, Google Machine Learning Crash Course
text:
## Overfitting and Underfitting
Overfitting means creating a model that matches, or memorizes, the training set so closely that the model fails to make correct predictions on new data. Generalization is the opposite of overfitting: a model that generalizes well makes accurate predictions on previously unseen data, and this is the primary goal of machine learning. An underfit model fails to perform well even on the training data, the opposite problem on the performance spectrum. Overfitting stems from two primary causes: training data that inadequately represents real world conditions, or a model that is excessively complex.

## Three Conditions for Good Generalization
Models that generalize effectively rely on three assumptions. First, examples must be independent and identically distributed, a formal way of saying your examples cannot influence each other. Second, the distribution is stationary, meaning the dataset does not change significantly over time. Third, examples are drawn from the same distribution across the training, validation, and test partitions, which should maintain similar statistical distributions.

## Detecting Overfitting
A generalization curve plots loss for both the training and validation sets over training. When the training loss keeps decreasing while the validation loss starts to increase, the two curves diverge, which strongly suggests overfitting. A guiding heuristic is that simpler models tend to generalize better than complex ones, so all else being equal, prefer the simpler model. A hard rule is to never train on the test data: a suspiciously high accuracy is a warning sign that you have accidentally trained on the test set.

title: Regularization for Simplicity (L2), Google Machine Learning Crash Course
text:
Regularization combats overfitting by penalizing model complexity rather than only minimizing loss. Instead of training to minimize loss alone, the model trains to minimize loss plus lambda times complexity, a strategy known as structural risk minimization.

## L2 Regularization
L2 regularization, also called ridge, defines complexity as the sum of the squares of all the model weights, w1 squared plus w2 squared and so on. This penalty encourages weights toward 0 but never pushes them all the way to zero, so all features are retained while their influence is minimized. Weights close to zero have little effect on complexity, while outlier weights can have a large effect.

## The Lambda Regularization Rate
Model developers tune the balance between fitting the data and staying simple through the regularization rate lambda. A high lambda strengthens regularization, reducing overfitting risk, and produces a weight histogram that looks like a normal distribution centered on zero. A low lambda weakens regularization, increasing overfitting risk, and yields a flatter weight distribution. There is a tension with learning rate: a high learning rate often pulls weights away from zero while a high regularization rate pushes them toward zero, so the two must be balanced. Early stopping, ending training before full convergence, is a quick but rarely optimal alternative form of regularization.

title: Classification: ROC and AUC, Google Machine Learning Crash Course
text:
## The ROC Curve
The receiver operating characteristic curve visualizes a classification model's performance across all possible classification thresholds. It plots the true positive rate, TPR, on the y-axis against the false positive rate, FPR, on the x-axis, calculated at every threshold. A perfect model has a point where TPR is 1.0 and FPR is 0.0. A model that guesses randomly traces the diagonal line from (0,0) to (1,1). Lowering the classification threshold generally increases both TPR and FPR, moving along the curve.

## AUC
The area under the ROC curve, AUC, aggregates the curve into a single number that quantifies the model's ranking ability. AUC represents the probability that the model, given a randomly chosen positive and a randomly chosen negative example, ranks the positive higher than the negative. An AUC of 1.0 is perfect classification, meaning the positive is always ranked above the negative. An AUC of 0.5 is equivalent to random guessing. An AUC below 0.5 is worse than random guessing. Because AUC evaluates ranking across all thresholds, it is threshold independent, measuring the model's overall discriminative ability regardless of which decision boundary you eventually deploy. This makes it useful when the operating threshold is not yet fixed, though for heavily imbalanced problems precision and recall based metrics may be more informative.

title: Preprocessing data: standardization and encoding, scikit-learn official documentation
text:
## Standardization
Standardization of datasets is a common requirement for many machine learning estimators. They might behave badly if the individual features do not more or less look like standard normally distributed data, that is, Gaussian with zero mean and unit variance. The concern is that many elements used in the objective function of a learning algorithm, such as the RBF kernel of support vector machines or the l1 and l2 regularizers of linear models, assume all features are centered around zero and have variance in the same order. If a feature has a variance that is orders of magnitude larger than others, it might dominate the objective function and make the estimator unable to learn from the other features correctly. StandardScaler centers each feature by removing its mean and scales it by dividing by its standard deviation, and it should be fit on the training set and applied to test data, ideally as an early step in a Pipeline.

## Scaling to a Range
MinMaxScaler is an alternative that scales features to a given range, often 0 to 1, using the formula X_std = (X minus X.min) divided by (X.max minus X.min). MaxAbsScaler scales to the range minus 1 to 1 by dividing by the largest absolute value and is recommended for sparse data, since centering sparse data would destroy its sparseness. When data contains many outliers, mean and variance scaling is unreliable, and RobustScaler, which uses robust estimates of center and range, is a better drop in replacement.

## Encoding Categorical Features
Categorical features such as male, female or from Europe, from US must be encoded. OrdinalEncoder maps each category to an integer from 0 to n_categories minus 1, but such integers imply an ordering that many estimators would wrongly interpret. OneHotEncoder, also called one of K or dummy encoding, transforms a feature with n categories into n binary features where exactly one is 1. The drop parameter can encode into n minus 1 columns to avoid collinearity in non regularized linear models. A critical rule is that any transform fit during training must also be applied when making predictions.

title: Pipelines and composite estimators, scikit-learn official documentation
text:
A Pipeline chains multiple estimators into one, which is useful because there is often a fixed sequence of steps in processing data, for example feature selection, normalization, and classification. Pipelines serve three main purposes. Convenience: you only have to call fit and predict once on your data to fit a whole sequence of estimators. Joint parameter selection: you can grid search over the parameters of all estimators in the pipeline at once. Safety: pipelines help avoid leaking statistics from your test data into the trained model in cross validation, by ensuring the same samples are used to train the transformers and predictors.

## How Pipelines Work
All estimators in a pipeline except the last one must be transformers, meaning they must have a transform method; the last estimator may be any type such as a transformer or a classifier. Calling fit on the pipeline is the same as calling fit on each estimator in turn, transforming the input and passing it to the next step, and the pipeline exposes all the methods of the last estimator. For example, Pipeline([('reduce_dim', PCA()), ('clf', SVC())]) applies PCA and then the classifier as a single object.

## ColumnTransformer
Real datasets often have features of different types, such as text, floats, and dates, where each type requires separate preprocessing. Incorporating statistics from test data into the preprocessors makes cross validation scores unreliable, a form of data leakage. ColumnTransformer applies different transformations to different columns of the data, for example OneHotEncoder for a city column and CountVectorizer for a title column, all within a Pipeline that is safe from leakage and whose preprocessing parameters can be included in a search.

title: Tuning the hyper-parameters of an estimator, scikit-learn official documentation
text:
Hyper-parameters are parameters that are not directly learnt within estimators; in scikit-learn they are passed as arguments to the estimator constructor, for example C, kernel, and gamma for a support vector classifier, or alpha for Lasso. A search consists of an estimator, a parameter space, a method for searching or sampling candidates, a cross validation scheme, and a score function.

## Grid Search versus Randomized Search
GridSearchCV exhaustively generates candidates from a grid of parameter values specified with param_grid, and when fitting it evaluates all possible combinations of parameter values and retains the best. RandomizedSearchCV instead samples each setting from a distribution over possible values, which has two benefits over exhaustive search: a budget can be chosen independent of the number of parameters and values, and adding parameters that do not influence performance does not decrease efficiency. For continuous parameters such as C it is important to specify a continuous distribution, for example loguniform, so that increasing n_iter leads to a finer search. By default the search uses the estimator's score, accuracy for classification and r2 for regression, but an alternative can be given via the scoring parameter, and multiple metrics require setting refit to the metric that determines best_params_.

## Held-Out Evaluation and Nested Cross-Validation
Model selection by evaluating parameter settings can be seen as using the labeled data to train the parameters of the grid. When evaluating the resulting model it is important to do so on held out samples that were not seen during the grid search, so it is recommended to split the data into a development set fed to GridSearchCV and a separate evaluation set to compute performance metrics. Nested cross validation is the best practice for obtaining an unbiased estimate of the tuned model's generalization performance.

title: Underfitting vs. Overfitting (bias-variance), scikit-learn official documentation
text:
This example fits polynomial features of different degrees to data generated from a cosine function to illustrate the bias variance tradeoff. A degree 1 polynomial, a straight line, is not sufficient to fit the training samples: it cannot capture the underlying nonlinear relationship and therefore underfits, an example of high bias where the model is too simple to learn the true pattern. A degree 4 polynomial approximates the true function almost perfectly, balancing bias and variance. A degree 15 polynomial overfits: it learns the noise in the training data rather than the underlying function, an example of high variance and poor generalization to unseen data.

## Quantifying with Cross-Validation
The example uses 10 fold cross validation with negative mean squared error to quantify how well each model generalizes rather than judging by the fit to training data alone. The cross validated MSE is about 0.41 for degree 1, about 0.043 for degree 4, and about 0.22 for degree 15. The best generalization is at degree 4, the middle of the complexity range. The key insight is that a high degree polynomial can fit the training data almost perfectly while its validation error increases, which reveals that low training error alone is not evidence of a good model. Cross validation on held out folds is what exposes the difference between memorizing the training set and generalizing to new data.

title: Numerical data: Normalization (feature engineering), Google Machine Learning Crash Course
text:
Normalization transforms features to similar scales. It helps models converge more quickly during training, because when features have different ranges gradient descent can bounce and slow convergence. It helps models make better predictions, helps the model learn appropriate weights for each feature so it does not overweight features with wide ranges, and helps avoid the NaN trap when feature values are very high.

## Techniques and When to Use Them
Linear scaling, also called min-max, uses x' = (x minus x_min) divided by (x_max minus x_min) to map values into a range such as 0 to 1, and is best for data that is roughly uniformly distributed without extreme outliers. Z-score scaling uses x' = (x minus the mean) divided by the standard deviation, expressing each value as standard deviations from the mean, and is ideal when the data follows a roughly normal distribution; in a classic normal distribution about 68.27 percent of values fall between Z-scores of minus 1 and plus 1. Log scaling uses x' = ln(x) and is appropriate for power law distributions where a few values are enormous and most are small. Clipping caps extreme values at a chosen threshold so the model does not overindex on a handful of outliers, and it is often combined with the other methods. A critical rule of feature engineering is that if you normalize a feature during training, you must apply the identical normalization when making predictions, or the model sees a shifted feature space.

title: Machine learning is going real-time / ML in research versus production, Chip Huyen
text:
Chip Huyen stresses that in production machine learning, coding is a small part of the battle; the harder work lies in data, deployment, and continuous operation. Whereas research often optimizes a single metric on a static benchmark, production systems face many additional constraints.

## How Production Differs From Research
Data is not static: because distributions shift unpredictably, teams may have to deploy a new model very frequently, sometimes as often as every night, which contrasts with the slow timelines of research publication. Applications built on superior datasets tend to win, so data quality often matters more than a marginally better algorithm. Latency is a first class constraint: a model can be accurate yet useless if it is too slow, for example an autocompletion tool whose suggestion takes longer to produce than it takes the user to type the next character. Beyond raw accuracy, production ML must attend to fairness, interpretability, privacy and regulatory compliance such as GDPR, and the cost of serving.

## Deployment Is the Beginning, Not the End
Huyen emphasizes that shipping a model is the commencement of the hard work, not its conclusion. Ongoing production concerns include monitoring for data distribution shift and triggering retraining, compressing models for edge devices, and optimizing inference through techniques like operation fusion or reduced numeric precision. Traditional tooling also strains under ML needs, since line by line version control does not suit large datasets or model checkpoints. The practical lesson for a data scientist is to start simple, get the end to end data and serving infrastructure working, and plan for continuous iteration rather than a one time launch.
